name: Nehemiah
charge: Building the wall in fifty-two days with a sword in one hand; taking no governor's bread; forbidding usury; shutting the gates on the Sabbath; remember me, O my God, for good
summary: A cupbearer wept for the walls of Jerusalem, prayed four months, asked the king, and came. He built the wall against Sanballat with half the people holding spears, made the nobles give back the usury they had taken from their brethren, refused the governor's allowance for twelve years, threw Tobiah's furniture out of the temple, chased Sanballat's son-in-law out of the priesthood, and shut the gates on the Sabbath. Four times his prayer is the same: remember me, O my God, for good.
offense: Nehemiah prayed before making his request to the king and credited God's good hand for the permission, letters, and timber he received. He inspected Jerusalem's broken walls before calling the people to build. Under threat, he joined prayer with a watch, stationed families with weapons, and arranged a trumpet signal so the scattered workers could rally (Nehemiah 2:4-18; 4:9-20). He also confronted oppression within Judah. The nobles could not be allowed to impoverish the brethren while others labored to restore the city. He required restitution and refused the governor's allowance because the people's burden was heavy (Nehemiah 5:6-18). Later he restored the sanctuary chambers and provision for the Levites and closed the gates against Sabbath trade. Rebuilding included the ordering of conduct within the walls.
judgment: And the king granted me, according to the good hand of my God upon me. So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days. And it came to pass, that when all our enemies heard thereof, and all the heathen that were about us saw these things, they were much cast down in their own eyes: for they perceived that this work was wrought of our God. Think upon me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people. Sirach: among the elect was Neemias, whose renown is great, who raised up for us the walls that were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and raised up our ruins again.
offenseFull: Nehemiah prayed before making his request to the king and credited God's good hand for the permission, letters, and timber he received. He inspected Jerusalem's broken walls before calling the people to build. Under threat, he joined prayer with a watch, stationed families with weapons, and arranged a trumpet signal so the scattered workers could rally (Nehemiah 2:4-18; 4:9-20).

He also confronted oppression within Judah. The nobles could not be allowed to impoverish the brethren while others labored to restore the city. He required restitution and refused the governor's allowance because the people's burden was heavy (Nehemiah 5:6-18). Later he restored the sanctuary chambers and provision for the Levites and closed the gates against Sabbath trade. Rebuilding included the ordering of conduct within the walls.
judgmentFull: The wall was finished in fifty-two days. The surrounding enemies were cast down in their own eyes because they perceived that the work was wrought of God (Nehemiah 6:15-16). Threats, false reports, and invitations meant to draw him away had not stopped it.

Nehemiah repeatedly committed his service to God's remembrance. His account shows the fruit in a completed wall, restored provision, and corrected abuses. He sought God's regard for work that required continued vigilance even after its most visible task was finished.

verses.text: And it came to pass, when I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven,
And said, I beseech thee, O Lord God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments:

Let thine ear now be attentive, and thine eyes open, that thou mayest hear the prayer of thy servant, which I pray before thee now, day and night, for the children of Israel thy servants, and confess the sins of the children of Israel, which we have sinned against thee: both I and my father’s house have sinned.
We have dealt very corruptly against thee, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the judgments, which thou commandedst thy servant Moses.
Remember, I beseech thee, the word that thou commandedst thy servant Moses, saying, If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations:

But if ye turn unto me, and keep my commandments, and do them; though there were of you cast out unto the uttermost part of the heaven, yet will I gather them from thence, and will bring them unto the place that I have chosen to set my name there.
Now these are thy servants and thy people, whom thou hast redeemed by thy great power, and by thy strong hand.

O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king’s cupbearer.
Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven.

And I said unto the king, If it please the king, and if thy servant have found favour in thy sight, that thou wouldest send me unto Judah, unto the city of my fathers’ sepulchres, that I may build it.
And the king said unto me, (the queen also sitting by him,) For how long shall thy journey be? and when wilt thou return? So it pleased the king to send me; and I set him a time.
Moreover I said unto the king, If it please the king, let letters be given me to the governors beyond the river, that they may convey me over till I come into Judah;

And a letter unto Asaph the keeper of the king’s forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the palace which appertained to the house, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall enter into. And the king granted me, according to the good hand of my God upon me.
And it came to pass, when our enemies heard that it was known unto us, and God had brought their counsel to nought, that we returned all of us to the wall, every one unto his work.

And it came to pass from that time forth, that the half of my servants wrought in the work, and the other half of them held both the spears, the shields, and the bows, and the habergeons; and the rulers were behind all the house of Judah.
They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.
For the builders, every one had his sword girded by his side, and so builded. And he that sounded the trumpet was by me.
And I said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, The work is great and large, and we are separated upon the wall, one far from another.
In what place therefore ye hear the sound of the trumpet, resort ye thither unto us: our God shall fight for us.
So we laboured in the work: and half of them held the spears from the rising of the morning till the stars appeared.
Likewise at the same time said I unto the people, Let every one with his servant lodge within Jerusalem, that in the night they may be a guard to us, and labour on the day.
So neither I, nor my brethren, nor my servants, nor the men of the guard which followed me, none of us put off our clothes, saving that every one put them off for washing.
And I was very angry when I heard their cry and these words.
Then I consulted with myself, and I rebuked the nobles, and the rulers, and said unto them, Ye exact usury, every one of his brother. And I set a great assembly against them.

And I said unto them, We after our ability have redeemed our brethren the Jews, which were sold unto the heathen; and will ye even sell your brethren? or shall they be sold unto us? Then held they their peace, and found nothing to answer.
Also I said, It is not good that ye do: ought ye not to walk in the fear of our God because of the reproach of the heathen our enemies?
I likewise, and my brethren, and my servants, might exact of them money and corn: I pray you, let us leave off this usury.

Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them.

Then said they, We will restore them, and will require nothing of them; so will we do as thou sayest. Then I called the priests, and took an oath of them, that they should do according to this promise.

Also I shook my lap, and said, So God shake out every man from his house, and from his labour, that performeth not this promise, even thus be he shaken out, and emptied. And all the congregation said, Amen, and praised the Lord. And the people did according to this promise.

Moreover from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year even unto the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that is, twelve years, I and my brethren have not eaten the bread of the governor.

But the former governors that had been before me were chargeable unto the people, and had taken of them bread and wine, beside forty shekels of silver; yea, even their servants bare rule over the people: but so did not I, because of the fear of God.
Yea, also I continued in the work of this wall, neither bought we any land: and all my servants were gathered thither unto the work.
Moreover there were at my table an hundred and fifty of the Jews and rulers, beside those that came unto us from among the heathen that are about us.

Now that which was prepared for me daily was one ox and six choice sheep; also fowls were prepared for me, and once in ten days store of all sorts of wine: yet for all this required not I the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon this people.
Think upon me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people.
So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days.

And it came to pass, that when all our enemies heard thereof, and all the heathen that were about us saw these things, they were much cast down in their own eyes: for they perceived that this work was wrought of our God.

In those days saw I in Judah some treading wine presses on the sabbath, and bringing in sheaves, and lading asses; as also wine, grapes, and figs, and all manner of burdens, which they brought into Jerusalem on the sabbath day: and I testified against them in the day wherein they sold victuals.
There dwelt men of Tyre also therein, which brought fish, and all manner of ware, and sold on the sabbath unto the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem.
Then I contended with the nobles of Judah, and said unto them, What evil thing is this that ye do, and profane the sabbath day?
Did not your fathers thus, and did not our God bring all this evil upon us, and upon this city? yet ye bring more wrath upon Israel by profaning the sabbath.

And it came to pass, that when the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the sabbath, I commanded that the gates should be shut, and charged that they should not be opened till after the sabbath: and some of my servants set I at the gates, that there should no burden be brought in on the sabbath day.
So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice.
Then I testified against them, and said unto them, Why lodge ye about the wall? if ye do so again, I will lay hands on you. From that time forth came they no more on the sabbath.

And I commanded the Levites that they should cleanse themselves, and that they should come and keep the gates, to sanctify the sabbath day. Remember me, O my God, concerning this also, and spare me according to the greatness of thy mercy.
Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business;
And for the wood offering, at times appointed, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.
And among the elect was Neemias, whose renown is great, who raised up for us the walls that were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and raised up our ruins again.

entries.commentary: These are the words of Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah. In the month Chisleu, in the twentieth year, as he was in the palace, Hanani one of his brethren comes with certain men of Judah, and Nehemiah asks concerning the Jews that had escaped the captivity and concerning Jerusalem. They tell him the remnant left of the captivity in the province are in great affliction and reproach, the wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are burned with fire.

When Nehemiah hears these words he sits down, weeps, mourns certain days, and fasts and prays before the God of heaven. He beseeches the Lord God of heaven, the great and terrible God that keeps covenant and mercy for them that love him and keep his commandments, that his ear would be attentive and his eyes open. He asks that the Most High hear the prayer he prays day and night for the children of Israel, and he confesses the sins of the children of Israel which they have sinned, both himself and his father's house.

He confesses they have dealt very corruptly and not kept the commandments, statutes, or judgments the Most High commanded his servant Moses. He pleads the word the Most High commanded Moses, that if they transgress he will scatter them abroad among the nations, but if they turn and keep his commandments and do them, though they were cast out to the uttermost part of heaven, he will gather them from thence and bring them to the place he has chosen to set his name. This is Nehemiah quoting [Deuteronomy 28](/bible/deuteronomy/28), holding the Most High to what Moses had already taught in the wilderness, both the scattering and the gathering. -

These are the servants and the people whom the Most High has redeemed by his great power and strong hand, and Nehemiah asks that the Lord's ear be attentive to the prayer of his servant and of the servants who desire to fear his name. He asks the Most High to prosper his servant this day and grant him mercy in the sight of this man, for he was the king's cupbearer, whose job was to serve the wine and keep a joyous countenance before the king.

In the month Nisan in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, wine is before him and Nehemiah takes up the wine and gives it to the king. This is Artaxerxes the first, the king that came after Ahasuerus of the book of Esther. Nehemiah had not before been sad in the king's presence, for a cupbearer must be of a cheerful countenance, so the king asks why his countenance is sad seeing he is not sick, saying this is nothing but sorrow of heart, and Nehemiah is very sore afraid.

Nehemiah answers, Let the king live for ever, why should not his countenance be sad when the city, the place of his fathers' sepulchres, lies waste and its gates are consumed with fire. The king asks what request he makes, and Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven before he answers, seeking the Most High even in that moment before the king.

Nehemiah asks that if it please the king and if his servant have found favour, the king would send him to Judah, to the city of his fathers' sepulchres, that he may build it. The king, the queen also sitting by him, asks how long his journey would be and when he would return, so Nehemiah sets him a time, and it pleased the king to send him.

Nehemiah asks for letters to the governors beyond the river to convey him until he comes into Judah, and a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king's forest to give him timber for the beams of the gates, the wall, and the house he would enter. The king grants him all this according to the good hand of his God upon him. Nehemiah had already prayed, and the Most High heard him and put it upon the king's heart to allow him to go. -

Nehemiah comes to the governors beyond the river and gives them the king's letters, and the king had sent captains of the army and horsemen with him, an armed escort to see him safe. When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, hear of it, it grieves them exceedingly that a man has come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, the same opposition seen when the nation tried to rebuild before. -

Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem and is there three days, then arises in the night with a few men, telling no man what his God had put in his heart to do, for saying too much could ruin the plan. He goes out by night through the gate of the valley, past the dragon well to the dung port, and views the walls of Jerusalem broken down and the gates consumed with fire, then goes on to the gate of the fountain and the king's pool. The rulers do not know where he went or what he did, neither had he yet told the Jews, priests, nobles, rulers, or the rest that did the work.

Nehemiah then tells them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste and its gates are burned; come and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem that we be no more a reproach. He tells them of the good hand of his God upon him and the king's words, and they say, Let us rise up and build, and strengthen their hands for this good work. What is admirable in Nehemiah, as in Ezra, is that he never says the work was of his own knowledge or wisdom, but that the Lord's hand was upon him, and he puts that same vision on the men around him so they strengthen their hands to help.

When Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian hear it, they laugh them to scorn, despise them, and ask what this thing is, and whether they will rebel against the king. Nehemiah answers that the God of heaven will prosper them, and his servants will arise and build, but the mockers have no portion nor right nor memorial in Jerusalem. There was no shame in what he came to do. --- Topics: [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

When Sanballat hears that the wall is being built he is wroth, takes great indignation, and mocks the Jews. One of the heathen rulers rises up against the work, treating the rebuilding of Jerusalem as something to be scorned.

Before his brethren and the army of Samaria, Sanballat mocks the feeble Jews, asking if they will fortify themselves, sacrifice, finish in a day, and revive the burned stones out of the heaps of rubbish. He makes his mockery in front of his army, calling the people weak, the same way the heathen today mock the men who go out in one mind to do the work of the Most High.

Tobiah the Ammonite stands by him and says that even what they build, if a fox go up on it, would break down their stone wall. The enemy despises the work as flimsy, but the builders answer by praying that their reproach be turned upon their own head.

The wall is joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work. This is the pattern for Israel United in Christ today, a people with a mind to work who understand the condition of their people and the mission to rebuild their minds. -
Nehemiah answers the mockery with prayer, asking the Most High to turn the enemies' reproach upon their own heads.

When Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites hear that the walls are going up and the breaches are being stopped, they are very wroth. The breaches are the weaker places the enemies expected would fail. When they hear those gaps are fortified, their anger rises because their expectation of failure is broken.
They conspire together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to hinder the work. Their whole plan is to cause the work to cease and keep the city from being rebuilt. -
The builders make prayer to the Most High and set a watch against the enemies day and night.

Judah says the strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, there is much rubbish, and they are not able to build the wall. Even among the workers the burden grows heavy and discouragement sets in as the enemy pressure mounts.

The adversaries say they will not be known or seen until they come into the midst and slay them and cause the work to cease. The enemies plot a surprise attack, aiming to kill the builders and stop the work entirely.

Nehemiah sets the people in the lower and higher places behind the wall after their families with their swords, spears, and bows. He arms the people by family and posts them at the exposed places, ready to defend the work.

Nehemiah tells the nobles, rulers, and people not to be afraid but to remember the Lord, who is great and terrible, and to fight for their brethren, sons, daughters, wives, and houses. The answer to fear is to remember the greatness of the Most High and to fight for the family and the people.

From that time half of the servants work while the other half hold the spears, shields, and bows, and the rulers stand behind all of Judah. The people labor and guard at the same time, knowing the enemies are plotting against the rebuilding.
Those who bear burdens work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other. Every builder keeps a weapon ready even while laying the wall, watchful against attack.

Every builder has his sword girded by his side as he builds, and the one who sounds the trumpet stays by Nehemiah. The trumpet becomes the signal to gather, keeping the scattered workers ready to unite at the point of attack.

Nehemiah tells the people that the work is great and large and they are separated far from one another along the wall. Because the builders are spread out, they need a plan to come together quickly if the enemy strikes.
Wherever they hear the sound of the trumpet, they are to resort there, for the Most High shall fight for them. The confidence of the builders rests on the truth that their God fights for them.
They labor in the work, half of them holding the spears from the rising of the morning until the stars appear. The people work from dawn to nightfall, giving the full day to the task.

Neither Nehemiah, his brethren, his servants, nor the men of the guard put off their clothes, saving only for washing. They are so serious about the work and so watchful that they stay dressed and ready at all times, of one mind to finish the wall, the same way the people are to be of one mind and one spirit today in the resurrection of the people.
There is a great cry of the people and their wives against their brethren the Jews. Even in the middle of the outside threat, a wrong rises up inside the camp among the people themselves.
Some say their sons and daughters are many, and they take up corn for them that they may eat and live. The people are burdened, having to trade for grain simply to keep their large households alive.
Others say they have mortgaged their lands, vineyards, and houses to buy corn because of the dearth. The famine forces the people to put up their property just to feed their families.
Still others say they have borrowed money for the king's tribute upon their lands and vineyards. The heavy tax drives the people into debt against the very land they depend on.

Their flesh is as the flesh of their brethren, yet they are bringing their sons and daughters into bondage, and some daughters are already brought to bondage with no power to redeem them. Their own brethren are enslaving them over debt though they are one flesh, one people just come out of captivity.
When Nehemiah hears their cry and these words he is very angry. The oppression of the people by their own brethren stirs his anger.

Nehemiah consults with himself, rebukes the nobles and rulers for exacting usury each from his brother, and sets a great assembly against them. He brings a great multitude before the nobles to make the point plain that lending against their brethren for gain is usury and wrong.

Nehemiah reminds them that he and his have redeemed their brethren the Jews from the heathen, and asks if they will now sell their own brethren, so that they hold their peace and find nothing to answer. The nobles are silenced because they have no answer for enslaving the same brothers others labored to buy back from the heathen.

Nehemiah says it is not good what they do, and asks if they ought not to walk in the fear of God because of the reproach of the heathen their enemies. Their conduct toward their brethren should be governed by the fear of the Most High, especially with the enemies watching.

Nehemiah says he, his brethren, and his servants might also exact money and corn, but pleads that they leave off this usury. Even those with the right to lend are called to give up usury against their own people.

Nehemiah asks them to restore that same day the lands, vineyards, oliveyards, and houses, and the hundredth part of the money, corn, wine, and oil they had exacted. He calls for full and immediate restoration of what was taken from the brethren.

They agree to restore everything and require nothing, so Nehemiah calls the priests and takes an oath of them to do according to this promise. The promise is bound by oath before the priests so it cannot be quietly abandoned.

Nehemiah shakes his lap and says so may the Most High shake out every man from his house and labor who does not perform this promise, and all the congregation says Amen and praises the Lord, and the people do according to the promise. A visible sign seals the oath, and the whole congregation agrees, and the people keep the promise.

From the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, twelve years as governor in Judah, Nehemiah and his brethren do not eat the bread of the governor. Nehemiah refuses the provision owed to his office, governing for twelve years without taking from the people.

The former governors were chargeable to the people, taking bread, wine, and forty shekels of silver, and their servants bore rule over the people, but Nehemiah does not do so because of the fear of God. The fear of the Most High keeps Nehemiah from the burden and rule that earlier governors laid on the people.
Nehemiah continues in the work of the wall, buys no land, and gathers all his servants to the work. He gives himself and his household to the labor rather than to gaining property.

Daily one ox, six choice sheep, and fowls are prepared for him, with store of wine every ten days, yet he does not require the bread of the governor because the bondage was heavy upon the people. Though he provides a table, he refuses to charge the people for it, sparing them because their burden is already heavy.

Nehemiah asks the Most High to think upon him for good according to all he has done for the people. Nehemiah was about the work and for the people, not the usery of the people, and he commits his labor to the remembrance of the Most High.

When Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arabian, and the rest of the enemies hear that the wall is built with no breach left, though the doors are not yet set on the gates, they turn to another plan. With the wall standing, the enemies shift from open threat to schemes against Nehemiah himself.
Sanballat and Geshem send for Nehemiah to meet together in one of the villages in the plain of Ono, but they think to do him mischief. The invitation is a trap to draw Nehemiah away and harm him.

Nehemiah sends messengers saying he is doing a great work and cannot come down, asking why the work should cease while he leaves it to come to them. Nehemiah uses wisdom, refusing to leave the work for a meeting he knows is a plot to put him to death.
They send to him four times after the same manner, and he answers them the same way each time. The enemies keep pressing, and Nehemiah keeps giving the same steady refusal.
The fifth time Sanballat sends his servant with an open letter in his hand. The open letter is meant to be read by others, a public pressure tactic against Nehemiah.

The letter reports among the heathen, and Geshem says it, that Nehemiah and the Jews think to rebel and that this is why he builds the wall, that he may be their king. The enemies invent a charge of rebellion to frighten Nehemiah and give the king cause against him.

The letter claims Nehemiah has appointed prophets to proclaim him king in Judah and threatens to report it to the king, inviting him to take counsel together. The false report is designed to force Nehemiah into their meeting under fear.
Nehemiah answers that there are no such things done as they say, but that they feign them out of their own heart. Nehemiah plainly names the accusation as an invention of their own minds.

They all try to make the builders afraid, saying their hands shall be weakened so the work is not done, and Nehemiah prays for the Most High to strengthen his hands. The whole aim is to weaken the hands and stop the work, so Nehemiah turns to the Most High for strength.

Shemaiah, shut up in his house, tells Nehemiah to meet within the temple and shut the doors because men will come to slay him in the night. A hired man tries to lure Nehemiah into hiding in the temple, framing it as safety.

Nehemiah answers, should such a man as I flee, and who, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life, and says he will not go in. Nehemiah refuses to run or to misuse the temple to save himself, standing firm in his place.

Nehemiah perceives that the Most High had not sent Shemaiah, but that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him to pronounce this prophecy. Nehemiah discerns the false prophecy and sees the hand of the enemies who paid for it.

Shemaiah was hired so that Nehemiah would be afraid, do so, and sin, giving them matter for an evil report to reproach him. The scheme is to trap Nehemiah into a fearful sin they could use to shame him.

Nehemiah asks the Most High to think upon Tobiah, Sanballat, the prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets who would have put him in fear according to their works. He commits the hired accusers and false prophets to the judgment of the Most High.
The wall is finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. Despite all the plots, the whole wall is completed in fifty-two days.

When the enemies and all the heathen about them hear of it, they are much cast down in their own eyes, for they perceive that the work was wrought of the Most High. The completed wall shames the enemies, who recognize that this was the work and pleasure of the Most High.
In those days the nobles of Judah send many letters to Tobiah, and his letters come to them. Even inside Judah some remain tied to Tobiah, keeping a line of communication with the enemy.

Many in Judah are sworn to Tobiah because he is the son-in-law of Shechaniah and his son married the daughter of Meshullam. Marriage alliances bind some of Judah to the enemy, dividing loyalty within the people.

They report Tobiah's good deeds before Nehemiah and carry Nehemiah's words to Tobiah, and Tobiah sends letters to put him in fear. To the end the enemy uses those inside to pressure and frighten Nehemiah, the same way anything that can be done to stop the work of the Most High is still done today, and the people must keep their spiritual eyes open to see it. --- Topics: [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

On that day they read in the books of Moses and found written that the Ammonite and the Moabite should not come into the congregation of God for ever, because they met not Israel with bread and water but hired Balaam against them to curse them, and the Most High turned the curse into a blessing. When the people heard the law, they separated from Israel all the mixed multitude. The reading of the law produced immediate obedience, cutting off what the law said to cut off. -

Eliashib the priest, having oversight of the chambers of the house of God, was allied to Tobiah and had prepared him a great chamber where the offerings, tithes, and vessels had formerly been laid. Nehemiah was away in the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon, and when he returned and understood the evil, he cast all Tobiah's household stuff out of the chamber, cleansed the chambers, and brought back the vessels of the house of God with the meat offering and the frankincense.

Nehemiah found that the portions of the Levites had not been given, so the Levites and singers had fled every one to his field, and he contended with the rulers and set the Levites back in their place. He made treasurers over the treasuries, faithful men, to distribute unto their brethren, and prayed, Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and wipe not out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God.

Nehemiah saw men in Judah treading wine presses on the Sabbath, bringing in sheaves, lading asses, and bringing wine, grapes, and figs into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, and men of Tyre selling fish and all manner of ware on the Sabbath. He contended with the nobles of Judah and asked what evil thing this was to profane the Sabbath day, reminding them that their fathers did the same and the Most High brought this evil upon the city, and now they brought more wrath upon Israel. Buying and selling on the Sabbath is breaking the commandment. -

When the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the Sabbath, Nehemiah commanded them shut and set his servants at the gates so no burden would be brought in on the Sabbath, and the merchants lodged outside Jerusalem once or twice. He testified against them and warned that if they came again he would lay hands on them, and from that time they came no more on the Sabbath. This laying on of hands is not a blessing but a serious warning, and the merchants knew he was not joking. He then commanded the Levites to cleanse themselves and keep the gates to sanctify the Sabbath day.

Nehemiah saw Jews that had married wives of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, and their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod and could not speak the Jews' language, but according to the language of each people. Because the fathers were not truly in the house, the children learned their mother's tongue and customs instead of Hebrew and the law. Nehemiah contended with them, cursed them, smote certain of them, plucked off their hair, and made them swear not to give or take daughters in marriage with those nations, reminding them that Solomon himself, though beloved of his God, was caused to sin by outlandish women. -

One of the sons of Joiada, son of Eliashib the high priest, was son in law to Sanballat the Horonite, so Nehemiah chased him away because he had defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites. Thus Nehemiah cleansed the people from all strangers, appointed the wards of the priests and Levites every one in his business, and provided for the wood offering and the firstfruits, closing the book with the prayer, Remember me, O my God, for good. This is the book of records, and to see it as history rather than religion is to understand who these people are. -

text.text: And it came to pass, when I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven,
And said, I beseech thee, O Lord God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments:

Let thine ear now be attentive, and thine eyes open, that thou mayest hear the prayer of thy servant, which I pray before thee now, day and night, for the children of Israel thy servants, and confess the sins of the children of Israel, which we have sinned against thee: both I and my father’s house have sinned.
We have dealt very corruptly against thee, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the judgments, which thou commandedst thy servant Moses.
Remember, I beseech thee, the word that thou commandedst thy servant Moses, saying, If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations:

But if ye turn unto me, and keep my commandments, and do them; though there were of you cast out unto the uttermost part of the heaven, yet will I gather them from thence, and will bring them unto the place that I have chosen to set my name there.
Now these are thy servants and thy people, whom thou hast redeemed by thy great power, and by thy strong hand.

O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king’s cupbearer.
Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven.

And I said unto the king, If it please the king, and if thy servant have found favour in thy sight, that thou wouldest send me unto Judah, unto the city of my fathers’ sepulchres, that I may build it.
And the king said unto me, (the queen also sitting by him,) For how long shall thy journey be? and when wilt thou return? So it pleased the king to send me; and I set him a time.
Moreover I said unto the king, If it please the king, let letters be given me to the governors beyond the river, that they may convey me over till I come into Judah;

And a letter unto Asaph the keeper of the king’s forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the palace which appertained to the house, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall enter into. And the king granted me, according to the good hand of my God upon me.
And it came to pass, when our enemies heard that it was known unto us, and God had brought their counsel to nought, that we returned all of us to the wall, every one unto his work.

And it came to pass from that time forth, that the half of my servants wrought in the work, and the other half of them held both the spears, the shields, and the bows, and the habergeons; and the rulers were behind all the house of Judah.
They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.
For the builders, every one had his sword girded by his side, and so builded. And he that sounded the trumpet was by me.
And I said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, The work is great and large, and we are separated upon the wall, one far from another.
In what place therefore ye hear the sound of the trumpet, resort ye thither unto us: our God shall fight for us.
So we laboured in the work: and half of them held the spears from the rising of the morning till the stars appeared.
Likewise at the same time said I unto the people, Let every one with his servant lodge within Jerusalem, that in the night they may be a guard to us, and labour on the day.
So neither I, nor my brethren, nor my servants, nor the men of the guard which followed me, none of us put off our clothes, saving that every one put them off for washing.
And I was very angry when I heard their cry and these words.
Then I consulted with myself, and I rebuked the nobles, and the rulers, and said unto them, Ye exact usury, every one of his brother. And I set a great assembly against them.

And I said unto them, We after our ability have redeemed our brethren the Jews, which were sold unto the heathen; and will ye even sell your brethren? or shall they be sold unto us? Then held they their peace, and found nothing to answer.
Also I said, It is not good that ye do: ought ye not to walk in the fear of our God because of the reproach of the heathen our enemies?
I likewise, and my brethren, and my servants, might exact of them money and corn: I pray you, let us leave off this usury.

Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them.

Then said they, We will restore them, and will require nothing of them; so will we do as thou sayest. Then I called the priests, and took an oath of them, that they should do according to this promise.

Also I shook my lap, and said, So God shake out every man from his house, and from his labour, that performeth not this promise, even thus be he shaken out, and emptied. And all the congregation said, Amen, and praised the Lord. And the people did according to this promise.

Moreover from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year even unto the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that is, twelve years, I and my brethren have not eaten the bread of the governor.

But the former governors that had been before me were chargeable unto the people, and had taken of them bread and wine, beside forty shekels of silver; yea, even their servants bare rule over the people: but so did not I, because of the fear of God.
Yea, also I continued in the work of this wall, neither bought we any land: and all my servants were gathered thither unto the work.
Moreover there were at my table an hundred and fifty of the Jews and rulers, beside those that came unto us from among the heathen that are about us.

Now that which was prepared for me daily was one ox and six choice sheep; also fowls were prepared for me, and once in ten days store of all sorts of wine: yet for all this required not I the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon this people.
Think upon me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people.
So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days.

And it came to pass, that when all our enemies heard thereof, and all the heathen that were about us saw these things, they were much cast down in their own eyes: for they perceived that this work was wrought of our God.

In those days saw I in Judah some treading wine presses on the sabbath, and bringing in sheaves, and lading asses; as also wine, grapes, and figs, and all manner of burdens, which they brought into Jerusalem on the sabbath day: and I testified against them in the day wherein they sold victuals.
There dwelt men of Tyre also therein, which brought fish, and all manner of ware, and sold on the sabbath unto the children of Judah, and in Jerusalem.
Then I contended with the nobles of Judah, and said unto them, What evil thing is this that ye do, and profane the sabbath day?
Did not your fathers thus, and did not our God bring all this evil upon us, and upon this city? yet ye bring more wrath upon Israel by profaning the sabbath.

And it came to pass, that when the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the sabbath, I commanded that the gates should be shut, and charged that they should not be opened till after the sabbath: and some of my servants set I at the gates, that there should no burden be brought in on the sabbath day.
So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice.
Then I testified against them, and said unto them, Why lodge ye about the wall? if ye do so again, I will lay hands on you. From that time forth came they no more on the sabbath.

And I commanded the Levites that they should cleanse themselves, and that they should come and keep the gates, to sanctify the sabbath day. Remember me, O my God, concerning this also, and spare me according to the greatness of thy mercy.
Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business;
And for the wood offering, at times appointed, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.
And among the elect was Neemias, whose renown is great, who raised up for us the walls that were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and raised up our ruins again.
